David commits adultery (verses 1–5)

Consider what led David into this serious sin.

First, he neglected his responsibilities. He remained in Jerusalem when his duty called him elsewhere.

When we leave the path of our duty, we place ourselves in the path of temptation.

Second, he chose an easy, idle life. Laziness gives the tempter an advantage.

Third, he allowed his eyes to wander. He had not made a covenant with his eyes as Job had—or had forgotten that promise.

Consider also the steps by which one sin led to another.

Sin is a downhill path.

Once people begin doing wrong, they often find it very difficult to stop.

Consider how much worse David's sin became because of the responsibilities and privileges he possessed.

How could he rebuke or punish others for conduct that he himself knowingly practiced?

David tries to conceal his wrongdoing (verses 6–13)

Giving way to sin hardens the heart and provokes the Holy Spirit to withdraw.

Taking away someone's ability to reason rightly is worse than taking away that person's money.

And enticing someone to sin is worse than bringing that person into any ordinary worldly trouble.

David arranges Uriah's death (verses 14–27)

Adultery often leads to murder.

One wicked act may be used to conceal another.

We should dread even the beginning of sin because no one knows where it may end.

Can someone who truly believes act this way?

Can a person committing such crimes really be God's child?

Henry teaches that even if God's saving grace is not finally lost in such a terrible fall, the assurance and comfort of grace must be suspended.

David's spiritual vigor and joy in religion were, for the time, destroyed.

No person living in such deliberate wrongdoing can reasonably claim to possess evidence that he or she is a genuine believer.

The greater a person's confidence while sunk in sin, the more that confidence is presumption and hypocrisy.

Someone resembling David only in his transgressions must not use David's story to reassure himself that he is merely a temporarily fallen believer.

He must first follow David in humiliation, repentance and the other exceptional graces of his character.

Opponents of Christianity should not say, “These are the fruits of faith.”

No.

David's crimes were the fruit of corrupt human nature.

We should all watch against the earliest movements of self-indulgence and keep far away from evil.

Yet with the Lord there is mercy and abundant redemption.

He will not reject a humble, repentant believer or allow Satan to snatch his sheep from his hand.

God restores his people in a way that makes his hatred of their sins clear.

In this way, no one who takes his word seriously will be encouraged to abuse the comfort of divine forgiveness.

Giving way to sin hardens the heart, and provokes the departure of the Holy Spirit. Robbing a man of his reason, is worse than robbing him of his money; and drawing him into sin, is worse than drawing him into any wordly trouble whatever.
[2Sam.11.14-2Sam.11.27]
Verses 14-27
Adulteries often occasion murders, and one wickedness is sought to be covered by another. The beginnings of sin are much to be dreaded; for who knows where they will end? Can a real believer ever tread this path? Can such a person be indeed a child of God? Though grace be not lost in such an awful case, the assurance and consolation of it must be suspended. All David's life, spirituality, and comfort in religion, we may be sure were lost. No man in such a case can have evidence to be satisfied that he is a believer. The higher a man's confidence is, who has sunk in wickedness, the greater his presumption and hypocrisy. Let not any one who resembles David in nothing but his transgressions, bolster up his confidence with this example. Let him follow David in his humiliation, repentance, and his other eminent graces, before he thinks himself only a backslider, and not a hypocrite. Let no opposer of the truth say, These are the fruits of faith! No; they are the effects of corrupt nature. Let us all watch against the beginnings of self-indulgence, and keep at the utmost distance from all evil. But with the Lord there is mercy and plenteous redemption. He will cast out no humble, penitent believer; nor will he suffer Satan to pluck his sheep out of his hand. Yet the Lord will recover his people, in such a way as will mark his abhorrence of their crimes, to hinder all who regard his word from abusing the encouragements of his mercy.

Nathan confronts David (verses 1–14)

God will not allow his own people to remain undisturbed in sin.

Through a parable, Nathan led David to pronounce judgment upon himself.

Those who correct others need wisdom and care in choosing how to speak.

But once Nathan applied his story, he was completely faithful.

He told David plainly: “You are the man.”

God's response demonstrates how much he hates sin, even when it occurs among his own people.

He will not simply ignore it wherever it is found.

David made no excuses and did not minimize his wrongdoing.

He confessed it freely.

When David said that he had sinned, Nathan recognized genuine repentance and assured him that his sin had been forgiven.

“You shall not die” meant, according to Henry, that David would not suffer eternal death or be separated from God forever.

But David would continue to suffer the Lord's discipline during his earthly life.

He would not be condemned with the world.

One especially dreadful consequence of public sin by people who profess faith is that it gives God's enemies material for mockery and blasphemy.

David's case shows that even when sin is forgiven, God may still correct his children severely.

A fleeting gratification of shameful desire brought David many years of painful distress.

David's child dies; Solomon is born (verses 15–25)

Henry connects Psalm 51 with this period of David's life.

Although David had been told he was forgiven, he prayed earnestly for pardon, lamented his wrongdoing and remained willing to bear its shame.

He was prepared to remember it repeatedly and receive reproof for it.

God permits us to pray earnestly for particular blessings on the basis of his general mercy and power, even when no specific promise assures that those requests will be granted.

David submitted patiently when his child died.

Later God compensated that loss through the birth of another child.

The best way to retain earthly comforts or have a loss made up in some other way is to surrender them willingly to the Lord.

God showed special favor to Solomon and directed that he be called Jedidiah, meaning “Beloved of the Lord.”

Henry expresses confidence that prayers for one's children are graciously answered both when children die in infancy—being well cared for by God—and when others live and are loved by the Lord.

David treats the Ammonites harshly (verses 26–31)

David subjected the people of Ammon to severe slavery.

Henry regards this harshness as evidence that David's heart had not yet been softened by repentance when these events occurred.

The more deeply we recognize our own need for the Lord's forgiveness and experience its sweetness, the more compassionate, kind and forgiving we should become toward others.

God will not suffer his people to lie still in sin. By this parable Nathan drew from David a sentence against himself. Great need there is of prudence in giving reproofs. In his application, he was faithful. He says in plain terms, Thou art the man. God shows how much he hates sin, even in his own people; and wherever he finds it, he will not let it go unpunished. David says not a word to excuse himself or make light of his sin, but freely owns it. When David said, I have sinned, and Nathan perceived that he was a true penitent, he assured him his sin was forgiven. Thou shalt not die: that is, not die eternally, nor be for ever put away from God, as thou wouldest have been, if thou hadst not put away the sin. Though thou shalt all thy days be chastened of the Lord, yet thou shalt not be condemned with the world. There is this great evil in the sins of those who profess religion and relation to God, that they furnish the enemies of God and religion with matter for reproach and blasphemy. And it appears from David's case, that even where pardon is obtained, the Lord will visit the transgression of his people with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. For one momentary gratification of a vile lust, David had to endure many days and years of extreme distress.
[2Sam.12.15-2Sam.12.25]
Verses 15-25
David now penned the 51st Psalm, in which, though he had been assured that his sin was pardoned, he prays earnestly for pardon, and greatly laments his sin. He was willing to bear the shame of it, to have it ever before him, to be continually upbraided with it. God gives us leave to be earnest with him in prayer for particular blessings, from trust in his power and general mercy, though we have no particular promise to build upon. David patiently submitted to the will of God in the death of one child, and God made up the loss to his advantage, in the birth of another. The way to have creature comforts continued or restored, or the loss made up some other way, is cheerfully to resign them to God. God, by his grace, particularly owned and favoured that son, and ordered him to be called Jedidiah, Beloved of the Lord. Our prayers for our children are graciously and as fully answered when some of them die in their infancy, for they are well taken care of, and when others live, "beloved of the Lord."
[2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.31]
Verses 26-31
To be thus severe in putting the children of Ammon to slavery was a sign that David's heart was not yet made soft by repentance, at the time when this took place. We shall be most compassionate, kind, and forgiving to others, when we most feel our need of the Lord's forgiving love, and taste the sweetness of it in our own souls.

Amnon assaults his sister (verses 1–20)

From this point onward, David faced one trouble after another.

Adultery and murder had been his own sins.

Now similar sins among his children began the punishment God had announced.

David had been too indulgent toward his children.

He could trace their wrongdoing back to failures in his own conduct.

That recognition must have made the pain of their sins still more difficult to bear.

No one should expect kindness from someone willing to attempt sexual seduction or abuse.

It is better to suffer the greatest wrong than to commit even the smallest sin.

Absalom murders Amnon (verses 21–29)

Several things made Absalom's offense especially serious.

He arranged for Amnon to be killed when Amnon was least prepared to die.

He also led his servants into sharing the guilt of murder.

Servants have been taught badly when they obey a wicked master against God's commands.

Children whom parents indulge without correction often become a heavy sorrow to their godly parents.

Such parents neglect their duty to God because of misguided affection for their children.

David mourns; Absalom escapes (verses 30–39)

Jonadab was guilty in connection with both Amnon's sin and his death.

People who advise us to do wrong turn out to be false friends.

After a while David longed to see Absalom again.

Instead of recoiling from him as a murderer, he began desiring his return.

This was a weakness in David.

Henry adds an important qualification.

God must have seen something in David's heart that distinguished him from Eli.

Otherwise we might conclude that David too had honored his sons above God.

Joab arranges an appeal for Absalom (verses 1–20)

Notice how the woman presenting her case to David appeals to God's mercy and to his kindness toward guilty sinners.

The state of sinners is one of banishment from God.

Yet God never forgives in a way that dishonors his own law or justice.

Nor does he pardon people who remain unrepentant, encourage further wrongdoing or authorize harm to other people.

David permits Absalom to return (verses 21–24)

David was inclined to show kindness to his son.

But to preserve the honor of his position as judge, he waited for another person to appeal on Absalom's behalf.

Henry sees in this a picture of God's gracious dealings.

God has compassion toward miserable sinners and does not delight in their destruction.

Yet sinners can be reconciled to him only through a Mediator who pleads on their behalf.

God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.

Christ came into the land of our banishment in order to bring us back to God.

Absalom's outward beauty (verses 25–27)

Nothing is said about Absalom's wisdom or devotion to God.

The passage praises only his physical appearance.

What poor praise for someone who possesses no greater virtue!

A morally polluted soul can live in a handsome body.

Absalom had an impressive head of hair.

It was so heavy as to become burdensome, yet he preferred to bear its weight rather than cut it.

People rarely complain about something that feeds their pride, even when it causes discomfort.

May the Lord give us the beauty of holiness and the adornment of a gentle, quiet spirit!

Only those who revere him are truly happy.

Absalom gains admission to David's presence (verses 28–33)

Absalom behaved insolently toward Joab until Joab agreed to intercede for him.

His bold and insolent demand then secured what he wanted from the king.

When parents and rulers encourage such a person by yielding to his behavior, they may soon suffer serious consequences.

But if a human father's compassion could lead him to receive an unrepentant son, why should truly repentant sinners doubt the mercy of the Father of mercies?

Absalom's ambition (verses 1–6)

David allowed Absalom to display his wealth and rank.

Parents who encourage pride in their children do not understand the harm they may be causing.

Many young people are ruined by pride.

And people most eager to obtain authority often understand its duties least.

Absalom conspires against David (verses 7–12)

Loving parents naturally want to believe the best about their children.

How wicked it is for children to exploit that trust and deceive them through an appearance of religion!

Some prominent men of Jerusalem attended Absalom's celebration connected with a sacrifice.

Godly people are pleased to see others displaying devotion.

That very willingness to encourage religion can make them vulnerable to deception.

The schemes of wicked people and the cunning of Satan can draw good people into supporting evil plans.

David leaves Jerusalem (verses 13–23)

David decided to leave Jerusalem.

He accepted the flight as a penitent submitting to God's discipline.

Before an unrighteous opponent like Absalom, David could have defended himself and stood his ground.

But before the righteous God, he had to condemn his own sin and submit to the judgment following it.

He therefore accepted its consequence.

Godly people also worry about other people's suffering when trouble comes upon themselves.

David did not force anyone to go with him.

Those who preferred Absalom could join him, and they would share in his fate.

In the same way, Christ does not force people to become his followers.

David especially wanted to protect Ittai, a foreign exile and recent convert, from hardship.

He thought Ittai should receive encouragement and kindness, not danger.

But Ittai valued David's wisdom and goodness so highly that he refused to leave him.

A true friend loves at all times and remains loyal through adversity.

Let us cling wholeheartedly to the Son of David.

Neither life nor death can separate us from his love.

David sends the ark back (verses 24–30)

David cared deeply about the ark's safety.

It is right to care more about the prosperity of Christ's church than our own comfort.

We should prefer the success of the gospel over our wealth, reputation, ease and even safety.

Notice how willingly David placed his circumstances into God's hands.

Accepting the Lord's will is both our duty and our best interest.

Recognize his hand in every event.

Then, because you know that every event rests under his authority, you need not be afraid of the future.

David's sin was always before him (Psalm 51:3).

Yet it had never seemed as evil to him as during this humiliation.

He had never wept like this when Saul pursued him.

A wounded conscience makes suffering heavier (Psalm 38:4).

David prays about Ahithophel's counsel (verses 31–37)

David prayed against Ahithophel's counsel, not against the man himself.

He trusted that God controls the hearts and words of human beings.

Yet he also worked to oppose that counsel.

Prayer must be joined with lawful effort.

Otherwise we would be testing God.

No ordinary human being combines wisdom and simplicity so perfectly that nothing remains needing forgiveness.

But when the Son of David experienced every possible form of betrayal and cruelty, his wisdom, gentleness, honesty and patience remained perfect.

Let us follow him, hold to him and serve him in life and in death.

See how willing tender parents are to believe the best concerning their children. But how easy and how wicked is it, for children to take advantage of good parents, and to deceive them with the show of religion! The principal men of Jerusalem joined Absalom's feast upon his sacrifice. Pious persons are glad to see others appear religious, and this gives occasion for deceptions. The policy of wicked men, and the subtlety of Satan, are exerted to draw good persons to countenance base designs.
[2Sam.15.13-2Sam.15.23]
Verses 13-23
David determined to quit Jerusalem. He took this resolve, as a penitent submitting to the rod. Before unrighteous Absalom he could justify himself, and stand out; but before the righteous God he must condemn himself, and yield to his judgments. Thus he accepts the punishment of his sin. And good men, when they themselves suffer, are anxious that others should not be led to suffer with them. He compelled none; those whose hearts were with Absalom, to Absalom let them go, and so shall their doom be. Thus Christ enlists none but willing followers. David cannot bear to think that Ittai, a stranger and an exile, a proselyte and a new convert, who ought to be encouraged and made easy, should meet with hard usage. Let us cleave to the Son of David, with full purpose of heart, and neither life nor death shall separate us from his love.
[2Sam.15.24-2Sam.15.30]
Verses 24-30
David is very careful for the safety of the ark. It is right to be more concerned for the church's prosperity than our own; to prefer the success of the gospel above our own wealth, credit, ease, and safety. Observe with what satisfaction and submission David speaks of the Divine disposal. It is our interest, as well as our duty, cheerfully to acquiesce in the will of God, whatever befalls us. Let us see God's hand in all events; and that we may not be afraid of what shall be, let us see all events in God's hand. David's sin was ever before him, [Ps.51.3] Psa 51:3; but never so plain, nor ever appearing so black as now. David prays not against Ahithophel's person, but against his counsel. He prayed this, in firm belief that God has all hearts in his hand, and tongues also. But we do not find wisdom and simplicity so united in any mere man, that we can perceive nothing which needs forgiveness. Yet, when the Son of David was treated with all possible treachery and cruelty, his wisdom, meekness, candour, and patience, were perfect. Him let us follow, cleave to, and serve, in life and in death.

Whatever wisdom or assistance people provide, success comes from God alone.

When Ahithophel realized his counsel had been rejected, his frustrated pride became unbearable.

What breaks a proud person's heart may not even disturb a humble person's sleep.

Ahithophel recognized that Absalom's cause would probably fail.

He also feared that he himself would be punished publicly.

In despair, he ended his own life.

Henry describes this as a self-inflicted judgment driven by injured pride and fear, not as an example for others to follow.

Thus a mind filled with plans to do harm came to a wretched end.

Absalom pursued David.

But notice how God sometimes provides comfort and practical help through strangers when our own relatives have disappointed or betrayed us.

Our great King does not need our help.

Nevertheless, Christ promises to accept and reward acts of kindness toward the least of his brothers and sisters—those who are sick, poor or lacking basic necessities—as though they had been done to him personally.

David repaid evil with good.

Absalom had wanted only David to be killed.

David wanted Absalom alone to be spared.

Young people should remember Absalom's terrible end.

He hung helplessly from a tree, condemned and abandoned.

His death displayed God's displeasure against rebellion toward parents.

Nothing can finally protect people from misery and contempt except heavenly wisdom and the grace of God.

Ahimaaz prepared David to hear of his son's death by first encouraging him to thank God for the victory.

The more our hearts are fixed upon sincere gratitude for God's mercies, the better prepared we are to bear suffering that accompanies them.

Some interpreters believe David's wish to die in Absalom's place arose from concern about his son's eternal condition.

Henry thinks it more likely that David spoke without adequate reflection.

He criticizes David's excessive affection for a son who had lived without godliness.

He also reproaches him for disputing God's justice and for resisting the judgment that David, as king, was responsible for administering.

The rightful claims of public justice should have been placed above his private natural affection.

Even the best believers are not always in a healthy spiritual state.

We often grieve too much for what we have loved too much.

Let us learn from David's example to avoid indulging or neglecting our children sinfully.

But even in David's love and sorrow, may we see a faint picture of the Savior's greater love.

Jesus wept over, prayed for and died for sinful, rebellious human beings who had set themselves against him.

Sheba rebels against David (verses 1–3)

One trial follows another for God's people, for their good, until they reach the place where sin and sorrow are forever removed.

Angry people arguing with one another often misunderstand or twist each other's words.

Proud people insist that everything go their way or else refuse to give any assistance.

The favor of the crowd is not dependable.

Consider how quickly the cries of “Hosanna to the Son of David” changed into “Crucify him! Crucify him!”

Joab murders Amasa (verses 4–13)

Joab murdered Amasa brutally.

The more deliberate planning involved in a sin, the worse it is.

Joab readily sacrificed the interests of both the king and the kingdom to satisfy his own desire for revenge.

How could someone guilty of murder bring himself to pursue a traitor?

How could he enter danger so boldly when his conscience was weighed down with such guilt?

His conscience had become hardened and unfeeling.

Sheba finds refuge in Abel (verses 14–22)

A city that knowingly shelters a traitor exposes itself to judgment.

The human heart fares no better when it protects rebellious sinful desires that will not allow Christ to reign.

A wise woman acted prudently.

She satisfied Joab's demand and saved the city from destruction.

Wisdom is not restricted by social position or sex.

Nor does it consist merely in knowing many complicated things.

It consists in understanding how to act when a problem arises, how to prevent harm and how to secure a good outcome.

Many disasters could be prevented if the parties involved made an effort to understand one another and clear up mistaken assumptions.

The condition for peace here was to surrender the traitor.

Henry sees a picture of how God deals with the soul when it is troubled by conviction.

Sin is the traitor.

A cherished sinful desire is the rebel.

If we part with that desire and cast away the wrongdoing, we can find peace.

There is no peace with God while we insist on protecting rebellion against him.

David's officers (verses 23–26)

This passage describes David's court after he regained his throne.

It is good when competent people are appointed to carry out public duties.

Let everyone who receives responsibility seek to carry it out faithfully, as a servant of the Son of David.
